transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2026-11-05 14:30 PT
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Patel (Redwood SE), Emily Wang (Redwood CSM); Dr. Amelia Grant, Marcus Bell, Saira Khan, Leo Ortiz (NorthBridge Pharma)

Auto-summary: brief intake to understand closed-network constraints and update cadence. Customer heavily regulated, wants on-prem/private deployment with explicit offline update procedures and signed images.

[00:00] Jordan: hey everyone, thanks for joining — I'm Jordan with Redwood, this is Priya our solutions engineer, Emily from success. how's everyone doing?
[00:12] Dr. Amelia: good, thanks. we just want to walk through constraints up front. we run all inference in a closed network for regulatory reasons.
[00:18] Priya: totally, that's what we specialize in. can you help me understand the update flow you already have? is it USB-imported images? package sync?
[00:28] Marcus: right now it's very manual. we swing a signed tarball via secure courier to the datacenter, ops mount it to an air‑gapped host and run checks. it's slow, and patch windows are a pain.
[00:38] Priya: ok, that's helpful. Redwood supports an offline image workflow — signed images, checksum verification, and we can integrate with customer KMS/HSM for key provisioning. couple of questions: do you require HSM-backed signing on‑prem or is an external KMS acceptable?
[00:54] Saira: compliance wants HSM on our end. remote KMS calls out are not allowed without special approvals.
[01:02] Jordan: understood. we can support customers who keep keys in their HSM and only distribute signed artifacts. the runtime will verify signatures locally before deployment.
[01:12] Dr. Amelia: great. what about model updates? we need to pin model versions in case we need to reproduce FDA submission results.
[01:20] Priya: we do model version pinning and hermetic deploys. you can pin a specific model+tokenizer+quantization profile. deployments include a manifest with git/hash and a signed artifact.
[01:30] Leo: quick question — you mentioned KV cache earlier in the docs, how does that behave in an isolated env?
[01:36] Priya: the KV cache — sometimes the transcript here will say K V cash — internal cache is local to the node and persists across restarts if you enable persistent cache storage on your NVMe. no external cache traffic required.
[01:50] Marcus: hardware wise, our procurement team is looking at both H100 and A100. procurement lead time is 12–16 weeks. what do you recommend for steady throughput at low latency?
[02:02] Priya: it depends on sequence length and batching. H100 tends to give better perf on fp16/slow quant workflows and large batch throughput. A100 is fine and more predictable cost. also check NVLink and PCIe topology — multi‑GPU scaling will need NVLink for best throughput for some ops.
[02:18] Jordan: there's a cost/latency tradeoff. Redwood Optimize can run cost/perf sims on your workload to show expected tokens/sec and latency at different GPU counts.
[02:28] Dr. Amelia: I'd like to see that — we have long sequences for context windows, sometimes 8–10k tokens.
[02:34] Priya: ok, that changes the kernel selection. we also support quantization options; with 4-bit quant you'll save memory but may see slight quality deltas — we can evaluate with your eval set.
[02:44] Saira: on the compliance front, we need full audit trails, immutable logs, SSO with SAML and SCIM provisioning, and retention policies for logs at least 7 years for some submissions.
[02:56] Emily: Redwood Console stores token-level traces and you can ship logs to your SIEM or keep an on‑prem audit store. we support SAML/SCIM and RBAC. retention policies are configurable in Private deployments.
[03:08] Marcus: and how about emergency patching? if there's a critical CVE, what is the expected turnaround in an air‑gapped site?
[03:16] Jordan: good question — we have a documented emergency workflow: we provide a signed patch bundle, validation scripts, and a verified rollback image. lead time depends on your internal approval; our fastest customers have a one‑business‑day urgent lane for critical patches, but that requires pre‑established approvals and an on‑call escalation path.
[03:34] Dr. Amelia: that urgent lane sounds interesting but we need to sketch the approvals.
[03:38] Priya: we can provide a template approvals matrix and an example change advisory board (CAB) ticketing flow.
[03:44] [04:00] Speaker 2: um, also curious about fallback — if your private deployment can't serve due to hardware failure, do you offer a hosted fallback?
[04:07] Jordan: yes — for customers who buy a hybrid policy we can route traffic to a hosted model as a fallback. for strict air‑gapped requirements that’s not allowed though. we can also set up a regional dedicated pool in a separate private VLAN as an intermediate.
[04:22] Marcus: our compliance team forbids egress in many cases so fallback to hosted might not pass.
[04:28] Saira: exactly — we won't allow PII or PHI to leave the closed net.
[04:32] Priya: noted. so plan A is fully on‑prem with image signing and local KMS/HSM. plan B is a fully controlled dedicated region but that requires additional legal review.
[04:44] Dr. Amelia: what about the update artifacts themselves — do you support delta updates or only full images?
[04:52] Priya: both. we can produce delta patches that apply to installed images and are signed. delta reduces transfer size which helps in slow courier windows. we also include checksums and chain-of-trust verification.
[05:06] Leo: can we see an example manifest and the verification steps?
[05:10] Jordan: yes — I will share a sample manifest and a verification script. we'll also include our recommended hash algorithms and signing metadata for HSM integration.
[05:22] Marcus: network topology — we have a segmentation between inference nodes and research cluster. we sometimes need transfer to the research cluster for model retraining but that path is controlled. any latency implications?
[05:34] Priya: that depends on where you place the inference runtime relative to the research store. if they're separated by a firewall we can pin model artifacts locally to avoid cross-network fetches.
[05:44] Saira: one more compliance item — we need tamper-evident audit logs. can logs be write-once-then-forwarded to our legal archive?
[05:54] Emily: yes. Redwood's logging subsystem can sign logs and forward to your archive. for the private deployment we can use WORM storage patterns and integrate with your archive connector.
[06:06] Jordan: quick note on monitoring — we surface token-level latency, per-route QPS, and model-level error rates in Console. for private sites we ship a local telemetry collector that you can keep behind the firewall.
[06:18] Dr. Amelia: sounds good. next, hardware lifecycle — we have low tolerance for downtime during model upgrades. how are rollouts handled?
[06:28] Priya: we support canary rollouts, A/B routing, and automatic fallback to previous model if regression is detected by your eval harness. rollouts can be staged per rack or per node.
[06:38] Marcus: example — if we roll an update across 10 racks, can we do progressive rollouts per rack?
[06:44] Priya: yes, you can roll per rack and set rollout safety gates like latency thresholds and error thresholds.
[06:52] [07:05] Dr. Amelia: what's the pilot look like? we want to validate accuracy and perf without touching production.
[07:12] Jordan: typical pilot is 2–4 weeks: week 0 hardware intake + image install, week 1 baseline perf and smoke tests, week 2 controlled load testing and evals. we measure latency, tokens/sec, throughput, and quality regressions against your eval prompts.
[07:28] Leo: are there any known gotchas for isolated NFS mounts or NVMe wear when using large KV caches?
[07:34] Priya: yes — persistent KV cache on NVMe can increase IO and wear; we recommend either enterprise NVMe with write endurance or an in-memory cache with periodic checkpointing depending on your risk profile. also ensure proper IO limits in the container runtime.
[07:48] Marcus: ok. procurement timeline — we aim to place an order by end of Q1 2027. does Redwood support a temporary hosted eval while hardware arrives?
[07:58] Jordan: yes, we can run a hosted pilot to generate the baseline numbers and then re-run the pilot on your hardware to measure delta. we'll factor both into the pilot pricing.
[08:08] Saira: legal will need to review data residency and BAA.
[08:12] Jordan: we have a standard BAA and can provide legal exhibits for Private deployments. I'll flag our enterprise legal for a follow-up.
[08:20] Dr. Amelia: any red flags you've seen with other pharma customers we should consider?
[08:26] Priya: common issues: late involvement of procurement (hardware lead times), not predefining emergency patch approvals, and underestimating NVMe endurance. also folks sometimes forget to pin their eval prompts for regression tracking.
[08:38] Jordan: we'll include an intake checklist — procurement, CAB, KMS/HSM access, and a testing plan.
[08:44] Marcus: what's the rough OPEX after deployment for support and upgrades?
[08:50] Jordan: depends on support tier. expect 8–12% of committed infra costs for a mid-tier support plan that includes 24/7 oncall and quarterly security reviews. dedicated capacity pricing or enterprise private licensing will be separate.
[09:04] Dr. Amelia: ok. last practical question: can you run offline model evaluation (no egress) so we can verify quality on our data before we accept a model?
[09:12] Priya: yes. we can run the eval harness on-prem behind the firewall. we provide a self-contained eval runner that outputs signed reports you can keep as evidence.
[09:22] [09:30] Jordan: recap — action items: we'll send security docs, sample manifests and verification scripts, a pilot scope, and schedule a hardware intake workshop.
[09:38] Saira: please include the HSM signing flow in the docs.
[09:42] Jordan: absolutely.
[09:44] Dr. Amelia: thanks everyone, this was helpful. we'll regroup after workshop scheduling.
[09:50] Jordan: thanks, we'll follow up with a calendar invite and the docs.

[End of transcript — meeting ended ~48m]
